power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Background: Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections in bronchiectasis airways result in poorer lung function, advanced lung lobe involvement, worsened life quality, and higher hospitalisation rates.
Despite high prevalence, little is known about P. aeruginosa population genomics, antimicrobial resistance (AMR) rates, persistence, and transmission dynamics in Australians with bronchiectasis.

Methods: P. aeruginosa (n=137) isolated between 2009 and 2025 from 59 Australians with bronchiectasis underwent antimicrobial susceptibility testing against 11 antipseudomonal drugs, whole-genome sequencing, comparative genomics, and in silico AMR determinant identification.
Data were integrated with 4,575 publicly available bronchiectasis-derived P. aeruginosa genomes to determine global phylogenomic and AMR determinant patterns.
Results: High AMR rates were identified in the Australian isolates, with 75.9% resistant to at least one antimicrobial, 19.7% multidrug-resistant, and 9.5% extremely drug-resistant.
AMR rates were highest (64.2%) for ciprofloxacin and cefepime (44.5%), and lowest for piperacillin/tazobactam (8.8%) and colistin (0.7%).
Phylogenomics uncovered several instances of within-host evolution, hypermutation, persistence, and multi-lineage infections.

Of the fifty-seven identified multilocus sequence types (STs), seven (12.3%) were novel, five were high-risk international clones (ST274 [6.6%], ST395 [0.7%], ST244 [0.7%], ST277 [0.7%], ST298 [0.7%]) and three were common global clones (ST253 [5.1%], ST155 [3.6%], ST260 [0.7%]).
No high-risk AMR-conferring mobile genetic elements were seen, although numerous chromosomal AMR determinants were identified.
AMR determinant prevalence was consistent with the global dataset, with no evidence of geographic clustering.
Our study provides critical insights into P. aeruginosa diversity in Australians 49 with bronchiectasis.
High AMR rates and chronic colonisation highlight the need to improve 50 diagnostics, antimicrobial stewardship measures, and infection control practices in this 51 neglected clinical cohort.

Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a leading threat to global health, with six priority pathogens, known collectively as the ESKAPE pathogens (Enterococcus faecium, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Enterobacter spp.), representing the greatest AMR burden (1, 2).

text.text: The environmentally ubiquitous ESKAPE pathogen, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, poses a significant concern across medicine, agriculture, and veterinary practice due its high virulence, capacity for extensive drug resistance (XDR), and association with poor clinical outcomes (3) (4) (5).

text.text: P. aeruginosa is particularly burdensome for people with chronic respiratory conditions like cystic fibrosis (CF) and bronchiectasis.
Bronchiectasis is characterised by permanent bronchial dilatation and distortion, resulting from a vicious cycle of infection, inflammation, impaired mucociliary clearance, and airway injury (6, 7).

text.text: With the global rise of AMR P. aeruginosa strains and occasional reports of pan-drug-resistant strains, treatment is becoming increasingly complicated for an already notorious and difficult-to-treat pathogen.

Multidrug (MDR) (i.e. resistance towards three or more antibiotic classes) and XDR (i.e. resistance to all except 1-2 classes) P. aeruginosa pose an increasing challenge in the treatment of chronic respiratory disease (13, 14).

text.text: Among the limited published studies, reported MDR rates vary considerably.

For instance, similar MDR rates of 16.3%, 16%, and 11% were found in a 2026 Chinese study of 306 non-duplicate P. aeruginosa isolates, a small 2022 Spanish study of 43 P. aeruginosa isolates, and a retrospective 2015 UK study of 155 participants, respectively (20) (21) (22).

text.text: There is a relative dearth of AMR data available from bronchiectasis-derived P. aeruginosa in Australia.

A recent study by Madden et al. found that Australian P. aeruginosa isolates from other chronic respiratory diseases can develop AMR in undetermined ways compared with comprehensively studied strains from Europe and the United States (25).

It is therefore a priority to better understand P. aeruginosa population genetics, AMR rates and associated genetic determinants, and persistence rates from bronchiectasis in understudied geographic regions such as Australia.

text.text: Whole-genome sequencing.

Genomic DNA was extracted from purified isolates by transferring a ~10 μL loopful of agar-cultured cells into 200 μL lysis buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 2 mM sodium EDTA, and 1.2% Triton X-100 [Sigma-Aldrich]), followed by bead beating in DNase-free 2 mL O-ring tubes (SSIBio, Lod, CA, USA) containing ~100 μL of 0.1 and 0.5 mm zirconia beads (Daintree Scientific, St Helens, TAS, Australia) using a Precellys Evolution Touch Homogeniser (Bertin Technologies, Montigny-le-Bretonneux, France) at 2 x 7500 rpm for 60 sec (with a 30 sec pause between cycles).
DNA was purified using the 'Gram-positive Bacteria' protocol of the DNeasy Blood and Tissue kit (QIAGEN, Clayton, VIC, Australia), commencing at the Buffer AL and Proteinase K addition step.
Extracted DNA was quantified using a Qubit 4 fluorometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Scoresby, VIC, Australia).
WGS was performed using Illumina NovaSeq X to generate 150bp paired-end reads at ~100x depth (AZENTA, Suzhou, China and Macrogen, Geumcheon-gu, Seoul, Korea).
Following genome quality filtering and assessment using Trimmomatic v0.39 (44) and FastQC v12.1 (45), species identification was conducted using Kraken 2 v2.17.1 (46).

text.text: AMR rates were high, with 75.9% (n=104/137) isolates being resistant to at least one clinically relevant antibiotic.

Specifically, 46.7% (n=64/137) were AMR, 19.7% (n=27/137) were MDR, and 9.5% (n=13/137) were XDR (i.e. resistant to all except one or two categories (13,42)), with the remaining isolates (24.1%; n=33/137) sensitive to all tested antimicrobials (Table S3; Figure 2).

Within-host evolution.
Among our longitudinal cases, phylogenomic reconstruction revealed a strong signal of within-host evolution in participants who were infected for at least 6 months (n=13/13 [100%]).
Within-host genetic distances ranged from 8 to 1646 accumulated SNP differences (Table S3), with an average of 1.16 substitutions per million base pairs/year, excluding two outliers (Figure 4).

text.text: In most cases, AMR rates did not worsen over time, consistent with the initial isolates often already possessing high AMR levels, and in some cases (P06, P39, P45), isolates became more susceptible over time.
Of the participants who developed worsening AMR, we identified several chromosomal AMR determinants associated with acquired phenotypic resistance.

text.text: Numerous studies have investigated AMR P. aeruginosa in CF, bloodstream infections, and nosocomial infections.
However, research detailing the prevalence and genomic epidemiology of AMR P. aeruginosa in bronchiectasis is limited, with a noticeable dearth of data from Australia.

To address this gap, we investigated AMR prevalence, underlying genetic mechanisms, population structure, and within-host evolutionary dynamics of P. aeruginosa isolates from a contemporary Australian bronchiectasis cohort.
Approximately three-quarters (75.9%) of our Australian P. aeruginosa isolates were resistant to at least one clinically relevant antibiotic, with 46.7% AMR, 19.7% MDR, and 9.5% XDR.
Fortunately, no pan-drug resistant isolates were identified.
Our MDR incidence was high compared to several prior bronchiectasis studies, including a retrospective observational UK study (11%; n=155 participants) (22), a recent Chinese study by Xu et al.

The isolate was recovered from an elderly participant on long-term nebulised CST with severely impaired lung function (FEV 1 : 39.5%) and a severe BSI score of 14.

CST resistance is predominantly driven via activation of two-component systems, frequently PmrAB or PhoPQ, which mediates the addition of positively charged moieties to lipid A, preventing the initial electrostatic interactions of CST (71,72,77,78).

We identified a missense mutation in pmrB (Val136Met), which was recently identified in an experimental CST evolution study (79), and a phoQ mutation (Gln263His), reported once prior in a hospitalised patient with a CST-resistant P. aeruginosa infection of unspecified origin (80).

text.text: Taken together, these substantial genomic adaptations drive a high rate of chronic persistence that closely mirrors CF cohorts, ultimately establishing a formidable barrier to successful immunological and antimicrobial eradication.
Our study has several limitations.

First, despite our isolates being collected from multiple tertiary centres, they were collected from the same subtropical geographical region (Southeast for a subset of participants, leaving gaps in our understanding of parallel within-host 568 evolution pathways, transient infections with different lineages, and additional transmission 569 and population dynamics.

Third, functional validation of novel AMR determinants, including 570 those encoding CST or C/T resistance, was outside of scope for this work, but represent an 571 important avenue for future research given the importance of these antibiotics in 572 contemporary P. aeruginosa treatment regimens.
Our findings shed important light on contemporary AMR prevalence, genetic diversity, and within-host dynamics of P. aeruginosa from an Australian bronchiectasis cohort.
We found higher than anticipated rates of AMR/MDR/XDR, including the first reported CST resistant isolate in our region.
In all cases, AMR was conferred by chromosomal mutation rather than MGE acquisition.

The detection of persistent infections, within-host adaptive evolution, and multi-lineage co-infections further highlights the dynamic and heterogeneous nature of P. aeruginosa in the bronchiectatic airway.
Our findings emphasise the need for accurate AST and genomic sequencing of P. aeruginosa from bronchiectasis airways to assist with the development of personalised treatment strategies.
Such efforts are needed to improve longterm outcomes for people living with bronchiectasis.

P. aeruginosa isolates (n=137) were obtained from sputa collected from Australians with computed tomography-confirmed bronchiectasis as part of retrospective (Bronchiectasis and Low-Dose Erythromycin Study [BLESS] [n= 42]) and prospective (BRONX [n=58], CERTAIN [n=13] or both [n=13]) studies.

The BLESS Study was approved by the Mater Misericordiae Ltd Human Research Ethics Committee (HREC/MML/89908); the BRONX and CERTAIN Studies were approved by the Metro North Health Human Research Ethics Committee (HREC/2024/MNHB/107113 and HREC/2023/MNHB/90934, respectively).

Site-specific approvals were subsequently obtained from the Research Governance Offices at each hospital site (Mater Hospital Brisbane, The Prince Charles Hospital, and Sunshine Coast University Hospital) prior to participant recruitment and P. aeruginosa isolation.
Participant population.

BLESS participants were previously recruited for a 12-month, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial that investigated low-dose erythromycin efficacy in adults with bronchiectasis presenting to Mater Hospital Brisbane (South Brisbane, QLD, Australia; Nov 2008-Oct 2010) (35,36), many of whom were re-recruited during the INFINITY Study (May 2017-Dec 2018) for follow-up.

The CERTAIN Study was an interventional, non-randomised, unblinded clinical trial that investigated ceftolozane/tazobactam (C/T) efficacy for treating P. aeruginosa exacerbations in sputumproductive adults with bronchiectasis (including CF) who presented to Mater Hospital Brisbane, The Prince Charles Hospital (Chermside, QLD, Australia), or Sunshine Coast University Hospital (Birtinya, QLD, Australia) between Jan 2024 and Dec 2025 (Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry [ACTRN12623000976684]).
The BRONX Study was patients performed spirometry at baseline, with BLESS participants re-performing spirometry during the follow-up INFINITY Study.
P. aeruginosa isolation.

BLESS and INFINITY bronchiectasis sputa, which had been stored for several years at -80°C without cryoprotectant, were plated onto Luria-Bertani (LB) agar (Becton, Dickinson and company, MD, USA) at 37°C with 5% CO 2 for 24-48h, which resulted in good (43/68 sputa; 63.2%) P. aeruginosa viability.

Prospectively collected BRONX and CERTAIN Study sputa were plated aerobically onto MacConkey agar (Becton Dickinson Pty Ltd, Macquarie Park, NSW, Australia) within 48h of sputum receipt, with any non-lactose-fermenting colonies subcultured for speciation.
All plates were incubated at 37°C for 24± 2h.

Impacted loci encode pathways involved nutrient scavenging, stress-responsive secretion systems, virulence, and cell envelope modifications, including the Vre virulence factor transcription system (PA0673-PA0676), Hxc Type II secretion system (PA0677-PA0687), chemotaxis (PA4307-PA4309), iron acquisition (hemO, exbB2, exhD2), and lipopolysaccharide production (migA).

Examination of within-host evolution signatures across all participants unveiled the most common loss-of-function mutations in genes encoding motility and attachment (structural flagellar and Type IV pili components such as pilA, pilB, pilW, fliC; 640 total mutations), lipopolysaccharide modification (e.g. wzy, wbpL, wbpM and rmlB O-antigen synthesis and pagL lipid A modification loci; 345 total mutations), virulence and quorum sensing (e.g. lasR and PA5438 master quorum-sensing regulators, exoS and exoY Type III Secretion System effectors or components; 145 total mutations), biofilm, exopolysaccharide, and mucoidy production (mucA or mucD-associated alginate overproduction; 106 mutations), and energyintensive iron and haem acquisition machinery (e.g. pchF, pchE, hemO; 93 total mutations) (Table 6%) compared to Cabrera et al., although Xu et al. reported substantially lower aminoglycoside AMR (TOB 2.0%, AMK 0.3%) than our cohort.

Ultimately, broader geographic differences in AMR rates reflect variations in local antibiotic stewardship and prescribing practices, coupled with the underlying genetics of circulating P. aeruginosa populations.

Given the low (<1%) prevalence of AMR-conferring MGEs in bronchiectasis-derived P. aeruginosa, our findings emphasise the importance of accurate and up-to-date AST data collection and AMR detection at local scales, and the critical need to identify chromosomally encoded AMR determinants, not just MGEs, in AMR determinant prediction pipelines.
